newsitem.title: USA: Coca-Cola Enterprises profits boosted by market share.
newsitem.headline: Coca-Cola Enterprises profits boosted by market share.

text.p: Coca-Cola Enterprises Inc. Wednesday reported strong fourth-quarter profits as the world's largest bottler of Coke and other softdrinks gained market share and saw revenues surge 29 percent.

The company, which is 45 percent owned by Coca-Cola Co., had earnings of $9 million, or 6 cents a share, in the quarter, compared with a loss of $3 million, or 3 cents a share, in the year-ago period. Revenues jumped to $2.12 billion from $1.64 billion.

Cash operating profit rose 23 percent to $287 million from $234 million, as volume sales in the United States grew faster than projected industry rates and net revenues per case rose while domestic costs fell, the company said.

"By focusing on the fundamentals of the beverage bottling business and developing integrated, local-market driven, product, package, and channel strategies, Coca-Cola Enterprises again increased share-owner value by leading the industry with significant growth in volume, market share, and cash operating profit," said Henry Schimberg, president and chief operating officer.

"Based on our current outlook for the competitive environment in 1997, we expect to generate 9 percent comparable cash operating profit growth that will translate into approximately 25 percent earnings per share growth," said Summerfield Johnston, Jr., vice chairman.

Bottle and can physical case volume grew by 4 percent in the fourth quarter from the year-ago period, after adjusting for acquisitions in Europe. That reflects 3.5 percent domestic growth combined with 6.5 percent international growth, it said.

Poor results by Coca-Cola's French and Belgian operation, which it acquired for $915 million in July, reduced fourth-quarter 1996 earnings by slightly more than 5 cents per share after tax. The company attributed this to a seasonal drop in consumption of carbonated beverages in Europe during winter, and fixed costs such as depreciation, amortization, and interest.

Coca-Cola said it expects the seasonal dilution from the French and Belgian operations will continue in the first and fourth quarters and for the foreseeable future. The seasonal effect will become even more pronounced when the company completes its pending acquisition of the Coca-Cola and Cadbury bottling operations in Great Britain, it said.
Under favourable market and weather conditions, the European acquisitions should boost the company's results in the second and third quarters, it added.

Based on the current marketing plans and competitive environment, Coca-Cola Enterprises said it expects the British, French, and Belgian acquisitions to reduce full-year 1997 earnings by about 5 cents per common share after taxes.

Coca-Cola Enterprises distributes more than 58 percent of The Coca-Cola Co.'s U.S. bottle and can volume. It is also the sole licensed bottler for products of The Coca-Cola Co. in the Netherlands, Belgium, and most of France.
Coca-Cola Enterprises' stock rose 75 cents to $55.625 on the New York Stock Exchange at mid-morning.
